der-row.title: Nominative Masculine (The 'Der' Row)
der-row.rule:
Welcome to the Nominative case! This is the default dictionary form of a word. We use **der** when a masculine noun is the **Subject** of the sentence (the person or thing doing the action).

Think of it as the 'Who?' or 'What?' is doing the verb.
examples: **Der** Mann liest. (The man reads. -> The man is doing the reading.)
**Der** Hund bellt. (The dog barks. -> The dog is doing the barking.)

die-row.title: Nominative Feminine (The 'Die' Row)
die-row.rule:
We use **die** when a feminine noun is the **Subject** of the sentence (doing the action).

Remember, German has 3 genders. Don't let the word 'feminine' confuse you—it doesn't always mean a female person. For example, 'die Tür' (the door) is feminine!

das-row.title: Nominative Neuter (The 'Das' Row)
das-row.rule:
We use **das** when a neuter noun is the **Subject** of the sentence (doing the action).

Neuter nouns are very common in German. Words like 'das Buch' (book), 'das Haus' (house), and 'das Kind' (child) all use 'das'.
examples: **Das** Buch ist gut. (The book is good.)

den-row.title: Accusative Masculine (The 'Den' Row)
den-row.rule:
Here is the first big change! The Accusative case is used for the **Direct Object** (the thing receiving the action).

In English, we say 'I see *he*' vs 'I see *him*'. German does this too. When a masculine noun receives the action, **der** changes to **den**.

**Crucial Rule:** ONLY masculine nouns change to 'den'. Feminine (die), neuter (das), and plural (die) do NOT change in the Accusative!
examples: Accusative: Ich sehe **den** Hund. (I see the dog. -> The dog is receiving the action.)

dem-row.title: Dative Masculine (The 'Dem' Row)
dem-row.rule:
The Dative case is used for the **Indirect Object** (the person who receives the direct object, or the person you do something *for* or *to*).

When a masculine noun is the indirect object, **der** changes to **dem**.

**Teacher's Trick:** Think **'M is for Dative'**. The Dative articles for masculine and neuter always end in **-m** (de**m**, eine**m**). You can also remember the Dative row is **MRMN** (de**m**, de**r**, de**m**, de**n**) — like the 'Mr. Men' books!
examples: Ich gebe **dem** Mann den Ball. (I give the ball to the man.)
Ich helfe **dem** Hund. (I help the dog.)

des-row.title: Genitive Masculine (The 'Des' Row)
des-row.rule:
The Genitive case shows **Possession** (whose is it?). 

When a masculine noun shows possession, **der** changes to **des**.

**Teacher's Trick:** Think **'S is for Genitive'** (the 's-case'). The masculine and neuter articles end in **-s** (de**s**, eine**s**). The Genitive row is **SRSR** (de**s**, de**r**, de**s**, de**r**).

**Crucial Rule:** Because it is the 's-case', you must also add an **-s** or **-es** to the end of the masculine noun (Mann -> Mann**es**).
examples: Die Farbe **des** Hauses. (The color of the house.)
